chief_complaint: runny nose, coughing, wheezing, and chest retractions
hpi_details: A parent brings a 1-year-old girl with runny nose, cough, wheezing, and worsening chest retractions.
ideas: Her parent thinks her chest cold has turned into early childhood asthma because her older cousin uses an inhaler for wheezing.
concerns: Her parent is terrified that she might stop breathing in her sleep tonight because her chest and ribs are pulling in so hard.
expectations: Her parent hopes she can receive a nebulizer breathing treatment right away so they do not have to be admitted to the hospital overnight.
social_hx: Lives with her parent or guardian.

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of RSV bronchiolitis is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Plan for RSV Bronchiolitis: Nasal bulb suctioning, hydration, monitor oxygen saturation, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: runny nose, coughing, wheezing, and chest retractions

Key HPI features: A 1-year-old female presents to the clinic with runny nose, coughing, wheezing, and chest retractions. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening.
Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for RSV Bronchiolitis.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out RSV bronchiolitis.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Viral pneumonia without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Poor feeding or worsening retractions would indicate need for escalation of care.
management_principles: Plan for RSV Bronchiolitis: Nasal bulb suctioning, hydration, monitor oxygen saturation
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with chief complaint of runny nose, coughing, wheezing, and chest retractions.
reference_soap.objective: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for RSV Bronchiolitis.
reference_soap.assessment: Condition highly suspicious for RSV Bronchiolitis.
reference_soap.plan: Chest retractions require prompt in-person assessment of oxygenation and hydration. Provide nasal suctioning and hydration; escalate urgently for worsening work of breathing, apnea, cyanosis, or poor feeding.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation and diagnostic markers of RSV Bronchiolitis
Select appropriate diagnostic workup for RSV Bronchiolitis
Implement evidence-based management plan: Nasal bulb suctioning, hydration, monitor oxygen saturation

teaching.one_liner: Infant with runny nose, coughing, wheezing, and chest retractions.
red_flags: Poor feeding or worsening retractions would indicate need for escalation of care

must_ask.say: Can you see her chest pulling in when she breathes, or her nostrils flaring?
How much is she feeding compared to normal?
How did this start, and how has it changed over the past few days?

must_ask.objective: Screen for risk factors for severe disease
must_ask.say: Was she born premature, or does she have any heart or lung problems?
We'll focus on clearing her nose with gentle suction, keeping her hydrated, and monitoring her oxygen levels — no antibiotics needed since this is viral.

history.answer: My daughter has been coughing and wheezing for the past two days, and today I noticed her chest pulling in when she breathes.
The cough started about three days ago and has become progressively more frequent and chesty.
It started as a mild cold with a runny nose and sneezing three days ago, and the cough started the next day.
No, she has never had wheezing or breathing trouble like this before.
She coughs up clear mucus and swallows it, but there has been no thick yellow phlegm or blood.
She coughs all through the day, but it disrupts her sleep and seems worse when she is lying flat in her crib.
She has prolonged coughing spells, but she does not make a whooping gasp and has not vomited after coughing.
Crying and feeding make her cough more and breathe harder, but cold air or dust does not seem to trigger it.
Yes, I hear a whistling sound when she breathes out, and she seems to be breathing much faster than usual.
Her chest and the skin under her ribs pull in deeply with every breath she takes.
It began with clear nasal discharge three days ago, followed by a cough, and over the past 24 hours the wheezing and fast breathing have clearly worsened.
She had a low-grade fever of 38.1 degrees Celsius yesterday and feels warm today, but she has not had shaking chills.
No, there has never been any blood in her mucus or saliva.
She has had copious clear nasal drainage and a stuffy nose since the cold began.
She cannot tell me if her chest hurts, but she does not clutch her chest or cry out in pain when coughing.
No, she does not spit up frequently, and she has never had problems with acid reflux.
No, she has not lost weight or had drenching sweats, aside from eating less over the past two days.
She is drinking about half her usual amount of milk because sucking makes her breathless, but she had four wet diapers today.
Her four-year-old brother had a runny nose and mild cold symptoms last week.
She attends daycare three days a week, and a couple of other infants in her room had colds recently.
No, nobody in our family or circle has ever had tuberculosis or a chronic cough.
No, neither of us smokes, and we do not allow anyone to smoke in our home or around our child.
No, she has never had eczema, seasonal allergies, or food allergies.
No, she was born at full term and does not have any heart defects or chronic lung problems.
I was worried her cold settled deep into her chest and triggered asthma, since her older cousin has to use a puffer.
Her ribs are sucking in so deep with every breath, and I am terrified she is going to stop breathing in her crib tonight.
I'm really hoping you can give her a breathing mask treatment to open up her chest so we can take her home safely today.
She has been completely healthy until now with no prior medical issues.
She has never had surgery and has never been admitted to a hospital.
She is not taking any medications, and we have not given her any over-the-counter cough medicines.
She has no known allergies to medicines or foods.
She was delivered at 39 weeks through an uncomplicated vaginal birth, weighing 3.2 kilograms.
She is meeting all her milestones, growing along the fiftieth percentile, and all her vaccinations are up to date.
There is no family history of asthma, lung disease, or immune deficiencies.

exam.finding: Alert but irritable infant in mild-to-moderate respiratory distress with nasal flaring and visible chest retractions.
Blood pressure 92/56 mmHg, pulse 128 beats/min, respiratory rate 48 breaths/min, temperature 38.1°C, oxygen saturation 95% on room air.
Clear rhinorrhea and mildly swollen nasal turbinates; mild pharyngeal erythema without tonsillar exudate.
No palpable anterior or posterior cervical lymphadenopathy; no supraclavicular lymph nodes palpable.
Visible subcostal and intercostal retractions; symmetrical chest expansion without focal chest wall tenderness.
Bilateral hyperresonance throughout lung fields without areas of dullness.
Bilateral expiratory wheezing and fine crackles with a prolonged expiratory phase; no focal consolidation.
Tachycardia with regular rhythm, normal S1 and S2, no heart murmurs or gallops.
No peripheral edema, cyanosis, or clubbing; capillary refill time is under 2 seconds.
